record.original_question: Assuming space is infinite, does it follow that the maximum possible speed is infinite?

evidence.quote: c) An Open Question now: If the space is infinite, is the maximum speed infinite?

artifact.self_contained_problem: Consider a hypothetical model of physical space that is spatially unbounded (infinite in extent). Within such a model, is the supremum of admissible propagation speeds of physical signals or particles necessarily infinite? More precisely: formulate conditions on a space-time framework (a set X representing space, with an associated notion of distance and a notion of motion/trajectory together with an assignment of an instantaneous speed) under which the assumption that X has infinite diameter forces the supremum of allowed speeds over all admissible trajectories to be infinite. Determine whether the implication "space infinite ⟹ maximum speed infinite" holds, and if so identify a minimal set of axioms that yield it; if not, exhibit a counterexample (a model with infinite spatial extent but finite maximum speed).
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open philosophical/physical question concerning the relation between the infinitude of space and the existence of a finite upper bound on speeds. No definitive mathematical resolution appears in the literature; the question as stated is informal and its status cannot be verified from authoritative sources.
